item.title: A Canadian Sketch Show Beats American Late Night to the Punchline
item.description:
Hours after Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary five days into the job, the Canadian satirical series “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” captured the chaos in a sketch posted online — beating American late-night comedy shows to the punchline.

Some 48 hours later, and a week before the rapper Nicki Minaj traveled on Air Force One to rally for President Trump in Michigan, “22 Minutes” imagined the MAGA darling as Ms. Zacharia’s successor.

In both cases, the creative team on the show, Canada’s version of “Saturday Night Live,” did not wait for their weekly broadcast. The polished sketches went straight to the show’s TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, attracting nearly 24 million views.

For the last 34 years, this sketch comedy show has reliably roasted Canadian and American politics, culture and quirks. But “22 Minutes” is having a renaissance buoyed by Mr. Trump — in particular his trade war, tariffs, threats and insults toward Canada. Television audiences are up, and social media viewership is growing rapidly.

“Social media has opened up our show beyond what I thought was capable,” said Stacey McGunnigle, a cast member and writer who has created and portrayed many MAGA women, most memorably Karoline Leavitt, Natalie Harp and, ever so briefly, Ms. Zacharias.

“The show’s been on a long time, and we can be the butt of the joke sometimes as far as what people think our demographic is,” she said. “But in the six seasons I’ve been here, more young people are coming up to us who love it and watch it all the time.”

The characters Ms. McGunnigle most likes to play are pro-life, pro-gun, pro-war and pro-push-up bra. “Too much makeup, no moral compass, a pathological desire to protect the patriarchy, and blonde. Terrifying!” she said.

The show, which airs Tuesday nights on the publicly funded Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, leans progressive but traffics in nonpartisan political satire — anyone in the headlines is fair game. Since Mr. Trump began his second term, the show routinely points its lens at the United States and its deteriorating relationship with Canada.

“This Hour Has 22 Minutes” is the nosy neighbor with permanently raised eyebrows.

Fans include Graydon Carter, the Canadian-born former editor of Vanity Fair and co-founder of Spy magazine.

“Canadians are feeling an uncharacteristic blush of patriotism,” he said. “And there’s nothing like friction and impending chaos to bring out the satirists.”

Ms. McGunnigle operates with fast-twitch newsroom instincts. As soon as Ms. Zacharia held her first disastrous White House briefing, she knew the show had to do something. “And that 14-minute press conference,” Ms. McGunnigle said. “I felt we weren’t going to have her for long.”

While they were shooting the piece a few days later, Ms. Zacharia was fired. Ms. McGunnigle immediately began improvising, turning a sketch about Ms. Zacharia’s disastrous first news conference into one about her last. A bonus: “Saturday Night Live” was dark that week.

“Stacey McGunnigle’s Katie Zacharia was superb,” Mr. Carter said. “But for her it was a bit like getting the coveted lead in a play that closes on opening night.”

The weekly broadcast averages 571,000 viewers, up 31 percent from 435,000 last season, with 25- to 54-year-olds the leading demographic. The “Meet Katie” sketch has more than 21.5 million views across social media, and the first Leavitt sketch more than 7.8 million.

Mark Critch, a veteran cast member and writer in his 24th season, plays Mr. Trump.

“We’re the quiet house next door, and the house on the other side of the fence, they have a lot of loud parties, and there’s always arguing in the yard,” he said. “We’re watching over the fence going, ‘Oh, my God, what’s going on?’ We get to observe, which is a good thing for comedy.”

Mr. Critch has taken his Trump to Greenland. He whipped up a “Quiet, Piggy” sketch after the president insulted a reporter with the phrase. As Mr. Trump, he fulminated over The New York Times’s exclusive interview with Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a cold open. In an attempt to rekindle Canada-U.S. relations Mr. Critch, as himself, met with Gov. Janet Mills of Maine, who implored him to ask Canadians to resume visiting her state.

“I mean God almighty,” he said, “Even with all the arguing that goes on, there’s nothing a Canadian gets excited about more than American attention.”

Drawing inspiration from the Trump administration isn’t entirely new for the show. What is more recent is the speed at which the show reacts to news. Without social media, the show, taped on Mondays, would struggle to stay timely on Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States.

“TV shows are big machines and you don’t want to be late to the party,” Mr. Critch said. “There’s another audience that we can get to right away. When something happens in the moment, now the whole building pivots.”

Mike Allison, the executive producer and showrunner, said more people tuned in as Canadian-U.S. tensions escalated. Especially amusing has been the opportunity for interplay between Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney, played by Mark McKinney, on the war in Iran, reverse psychology, and McDonald’s. But not every sketch needs a Canadian tie.

“When writers pitch Kristi Noem or Kash Patel, that’s us looking over the fence at all the crazy characters running the country,” Mr. Allison said. “But U.S. politics have become Canadian politics.”

“22 Minutes has the DNA of the knowing outsider,” Mr. Carter said.

It always has. Twenty-five years ago, “Talking to Americans” was a popular segment testing how little Americans knew about Canada. Highlights included a Columbia University professor agreeing that the government should stop putting senior citizens on ice floes to die, and Mike Huckabee, then the governor of Arkansas, congratulating Canada on preserving its national igloo.

Mr. Critch often hears from Americans who don’t realize the show is Canadian.

“They will say, ‘Oh, good, thank you. That’s what I feel.’ But then you’ll get some saying, ‘You don’t know anything! That’s our president! Shut up!’” he said. “Something I see that’s actually very Canadian is Americans saying they’re sorry. ‘I’m so sorry this is happening. I’m so sorry they’re saying these things about your country. We love Canadians.’”

item.title: An 80-Cent Plastic Pouch Is Saving Thousands of Women From Dying in Childbirth
item.description:
A few hours after she nearly bled to death, Husaina Balarabe was serenely unaware that her life had been in peril.

She cuddled her newborn baby, a lush-cheeked boy she had named Aabid, and showed him off to her sisters from her bed in a noisy hospital delivery ward in the northern Nigerian city of Kano.

Ms. Balarabe, a 26-year-old optometrist, had experienced a postpartum hemorrhage, a side effect of childbirth that is the leading cause of maternal death around the world.

She did not die because her midwife used a low-cost, low-tech intervention that was pioneered here and in other maternity wards in some of Africa’s poorest places, and that is now saving lives across the continent.

The device was a piece of thin, green plastic the size of a cookie sheet with a pouch at its end, called a maternal drape. It lay beneath Ms. Balarabe as she delivered, and the pouch hung off the end of the bed. The midwife who caught baby Aabid saw blood running into the pouch and quickly reaching and surpassing the danger level — 300 milliliters (or 10 ounces), indicated by a mark on the pouch

The nurse swiftly grabbed a cart stationed in the middle of the packed maternity ward, called for help and went to work. From the cart, she took a syringe of the drug oxytocin and injected it through an IV to get Ms. Balarabe’s uterus to contract. She added a dose of tranexamic acid, to prompt clotting. She massaged Ms. Balarabe’s abdomen, encouraging more uterine contractions, while another nurse started IV fluids to restore her blood volume. The bleeding slowed, and after a couple of minutes, it stopped altogether.

It was all so swift and smooth that the new mother had no idea there was cause for alarm.

One in every 10 women who give birth experiences postpartum hemorrhage, and at least 70,000 women die from it each year. Almost all of those women are in low-income countries; more women die giving birth in Nigeria than in any other country.

Maternal mortality is one of the most bedeviling problems in global health because — until recently — the main solutions have required skilled health care personnel to identify women at risk and to intervene swiftly when a delivery suddenly becomes dangerous. But there is no cheap or simple way to produce midwives and obstetricians, or to convince them to stay in underserved rural areas when they could earn more in cities or other countries.

Postpartum hemorrhage occurs after a baby is born, when the placenta separates from the mother’s body, leaving hundreds of blood vessels open and pumping blood. In a normal delivery, the uterus quickly contracts, and the pressure closes those vessels. But if that contraction doesn’t occur or happens too slowly, or if pieces of the placenta are left behind, blood pours out without stopping, and the woman can die in as little as 10 minutes.

Some bleeding is normal in childbirth. The reason many women die is that it is surprisingly difficult to tell if someone is losing too much blood. Research found that even midwives and doctors who have delivered hundreds of babies consistently underestimate how much blood a woman has lost.

“The amount of blood on the couch, on the floor, on the pads, on my clothes, on her clothes, is it 300 or 500 or 1000 milliliters ?” asked Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano who oversaw the Nigerian research into use of the drape. “A lot of times, we don’t realize the amount of blood that a woman has lost because we make a visual assessment and it’s very, very subjective.”

By the time those delivering a baby decide it’s time to act, it’s often too late.

The drape is now being rolled out across Nigeria. But it was only the first part of the intervention that saved Ms. Balarabe. Next came the series of treatments after the pouch became dangerously full of blood. None of those steps are new, but a few years ago, researchers tested what happened when they were all done at once — massage, oxytocin, tranexamic acid, IV fluids — and quickly. They found that, together with the drape, these interventions cut deaths from postpartum hemorrhage in hospitals by about two-thirds.

Previously, health workers had been trained to respond by first trying massage and then waiting 20 minutes to see if bleeding stopped. If it didn’t, they tried a drug and waited 20 more.

When all the interventions are done together, in what is called a “bundle,” bleeding stops quickly in most women. “It’s like turning off a tap,” Dr. Galadanci said.

If it doesn’t stop, the last step is escalation: getting the woman into an operating room or transferring her to a facility that has staff who can stop the bleeding surgically.

“We have not had one death from postpartum hemorrhage since we started this,” said Binta Garba, who has been the head nurse in the labor ward at Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital for seven years.

Eight or nine times each week, one of her nurses will spot a pouch with blood past the 300-millileter mark and shout, “Bring the bundle!” The person closest to the trolley wheels it to the bedside. “Everybody helps, and in a short period, the bleeding stops,” Ms. Garba said.

When Dr. Galadanci was recruited to be part of this research five years ago, she was skeptical: How could a flimsy sheet of plastic and a small procedural change in treatment save women’s lives? The research convinced her — and she went on a campaign to persuade Nigeria’s health minister to make this the national standard of care.

Now, pairs of midwife-trainers are visiting labor wards across the country to introduce the drape and the bundle. Often, they’re greeted with the same skepticism.

“I thought, We already give oxytocin and tranexamic acid, women still die — you’re wasting my time telling me about something we already do,” Kursiyya Shuaibu, one of the trainers, said of the first time she heard about the new procedure. Then she used it, and saved a woman’s life. “When you bundle it, it’s magic!”

Postpartum hemorrhage also occurs in high-income countries, but women are much less likely to die. They typically have one-on-one care from a midwife or nurse, as well as electronic monitoring of vital signs that can flag a problem early, and blood supply for transfusion is readily available.

Nigeria has high rates of severe postpartum hemorrhage because it has weak primary care. Sixty percent of women are anemic, and there is limited access to birth control. The average woman in the north has seven children, and her risk of hemorrhage rises with each pregnancy.

A quarter of Nigerian women never receive any prenatal care during pregnancy; less than half manage four visits. There is a critical shortage of health care workers throughout the system, from midwives who might screen for high-risk pregnancies to obstetricians who could safely deliver them.

Dr. Galadanci talks fast, walks faster and bristles with impatience to improve the care women receive. She believes the solutions to these basic problems have to be equally simple.

“The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite: It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems,” she said. “You don’t need a surgeon to come and save a woman. Or to teach you how to do a technique with something you have to buy from outside the country. No. You just need a plastic calibrated drape, and you have your drugs. And it’s done.”

The drape can only do so much, of course: The critical levels of understaffing still put women at risk. On a recent afternoon in the maternity ward at the teaching hospital — the best public hospital in Kano — one woman lost 600 milliliters of blood before anyone intervened. Another woman’s drape went unchecked for nearly 45 minutes after her baby was born.

The drapes used for the research in Nigeria were imported from India, and cost about $3 each. That was more than the national health budget could afford.

Dr. Muhammad Ali Pate, the health minister, wants Nigeria to make more of what it needs. So Dr. Galadanci and her team got in touch with a family-run plastic manufacturer in Kano that made plates, forks and containers for things like vegetable oil. Dr. Galadanci showed the chief engineer a drape: Could they make that?

The company made a prototype, but it was clear that any significant production would require custom-built machinery, which it would need to import from Taiwan. The Gates Foundation, which had helped fund the drape research, was eager to scale up the drape’s use, and offered a $600,000 grant. (The foundation has also backed companies in Kenya and South Africa, where the drape was tested, to manufacture them.)

In exchange, the company, Systs Engineering, agreed to sell the drapes for 70 cents each to the national health system. The war in Iran has since pushed up the cost of raw materials, so these days, the drapes cost 80 cents. The company is making them for all of Nigeria, and it has started to export to some neighboring countries.

Dr. Galadanci has now moved on to the next problem: The drape and the bundle are working well in hospitals, but 60 percent of Nigerian women give birth at home. Her research team is testing a kit for community health workers who attend home births. It has an absorbent mat, and when that fills to the corners, it’s a sign a woman cannot lose any more blood and must be taken to a hospital. The kit also contains the drug misoprostol, which causes the uterus to contract, helping to stop bleeding long enough to get a woman to medical care.

Still, the hospitals are strained. On a recent morning at a maternity clinic in the center of Kano, seven women gave birth in the space of a couple of hours. The lone obstetrician, Dr. Halima Ibrahim, had three urgent cases waiting for cesareans, and a lone midwife oversaw the delivery ward. One woman was whimpering through the contractions of her 11th delivery, while in the corner, a couple of student nurses used the flashlight from a phone to stitch another woman’s episiotomy.

But the drape helps. “It used to be that we lost a woman every month: You are left holding the baby, and the mother is gone,” Dr. Ibrahim said. “Not any more.”

This article is by far my favorite piece of news today. How wonderful that a simple, inexpensive item can save the lives of so many mothers. Dr. Galadanci is a miracle worker. The article also gives me hope that other major societal problems can and will be solved. Thank you for running this piece.

thank you for reading! We have a whole series of stories coming on low-tech low cost interventions making a big difference in maternal mortality – stay with us, as the podcasts say!

This is a great story and much needed reporting that has impacts far beyond a the countries now implementing this method. I worked on an ambulance for years, and every EMT and Paramedic are taught to gauge blood loss by estimating blood loss on the packing material or sheet, which is very inexact, having this drape available for vaginal bleeding, even non-pregnancy related ones, would jump start when the medications are delivered. Many ambulance or medical flights are hours long.

that's so interesting – that you had that experience as an EMT. One of my favorite things that I saw reporting (but alas could not squeeze into the story) was the quiz that the trainers use with midwives and nurses when they are introducing the drape and bundle. Of course the veteran staffers doubt that they have anything new to learn about catching babies – but the trainers show them a series of bowls containing blood; blood-soaked clothing; blood-soaked gauze and pads etc. and ask them to guess how much is in each bowl. In every case it's more blood than a woman can safely lose – but almost no one ever guesses the amounts accurately. They consistently underestimate. It's just really hard to do!

The article touches on this only briefly, but even the best interventions are only as valuable as the team that consistently implements them. When the clinical team found out that a woman had waited 45 minutes before her drape was checked, did they do a debrief, identify the failure points, and make an action plan to prevent it from happening again? The protocols, procedures, steps, and quality assurance components are absolutely vital, every time.

Hi Liz. Great point. It won't surprise you that no, there was no debrief after the 45 minute delay – I'm not sure anyone else noticed it (I was timing, out of curiosity). There were 2 nurses working in a ward of 20 women in active labor. At one point that week, I saw the security guard pulled in to help catch a baby (she seemed pretty skilled.) The gaps that occur reflect the very low level of skilled human resources available, and that requires a long term fix. Thanks for reading.

item.title: Israeli Claims of Iranian Chemical Weapons Divide U.S. Officials
item.description:
Israel has shared intelligence with the United States asserting that Iran is considering the use of chemical weapons against its adversaries, information met with alarm by some American officials and deep skepticism by others, according to U.S. and regional officials.

Some American officials see the Israeli intelligence as part of a pressure campaign by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government to persuade the Trump administration to return to major combat operations against Iran.

Other officials believe the threats should be taken seriously, given the recent array of warnings about Iran’s preparations to attack American interests.

Israel has shared some of the information with officials in Gulf countries. Several doubted that Iran was developing plans to use chemical weapons and believe Israel is trying to push the United States and its partners to return to a more intense phase of the war.

American claims about Iran’s chemical weapons, or its intent to build them, go back decades. In 2003, Iran acknowledged it had developed chemical capabilities during the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s but said it later dismantled them.

In recent years, the United States has publicly asserted in its annual unclassified intelligence assessments that Iran “likely aims” to continue its research and development of chemical weapons.

Iran has publicly denied having chemical weapons and previously described such allegations as psychological war waged by Israel and Mr. Netanyahu.

All of the people interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity, given the secret nature of the Israeli intelligence, the sensitivity of Iranian planning and the classified American discussions.

After eight months of war, the United States and Iran are in something of a holding pattern, exploring the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough and preparing for renewed warfare.

The debate over the new intelligence shows how tense the moment is and the potential for grave miscalculation. U.S. officials have said the Trump administration has no intention of using a nuclear weapon, but Iranian officials are not so sure.

The Needle, our live forecast, returns tonight

We’ll turn on our real-time estimates of who will win the Senate and the House once enough votes have been reported.

Waiting for estimates

Waiting for estimates

Mr. Netanyahu is fighting for his political survival after he failed to secure a clear path to forming a government in elections last week. Some analysts believe that the veteran leader may be seeking to use a security emergency as leverage to compel opposition leaders to join him in a coalition.

In recent conversations with U.S. spy agencies and other officials over the past two weeks, Israeli officials have portrayed the chemical weapon threat as more urgent than Iran’s ambitions to develop a nuclear weapon.

The Home Front Command, the Israeli military unit responsible for emergency response and issuing guidance to civilians, is running drills across Israel this week but is not including chemical weapons preparation as a major part of the exercises.

The command has also not issued widespread reminders to its officers or the public regarding safety guidelines for such a possibility, according to two unit officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the news media. The Israeli military declined to comment.

In recent weeks, the U.S. military has built up a vast arsenal in the region, with naval ships, fighter planes and bombers ready to launch a relatively short campaign of intense strikes after the midterm elections, should President Trump authorize action.

At the same time U.S. and other diplomats are trying to forge an agreement with Iran which would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, address Tehran’s nuclear program and put off further military action. The buildup of forces could be intended as much to support that diplomatic push as it is to prepare for a return to war.

Iran has intensified attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, hoping to exert maximum economic pressure on the United States ahead of its elections on Tuesday.

The use of chemical weapons is a particularly fraught issue for Iran, one of a few countries that have suffered the effects of them. During the Iran-Iraq war, Saddam Hussein deployed chemical weapons, killing thousands and leading to decades of health problems among some 100,000 Iranian veterans and civilians, according to Iranian experts.

U.S. intelligence agencies have long tracked Iran’s development of chemical weapons, which are banned under international law. Israeli intelligence agencies have told U.S. counterparts that they believe Iran is moving rapidly to develop the technology to put such weapons on a missile or to sneak them into Israel or another country to use in an attack, according to American officials.

For some American officials, the talk of chemical weapons threats from Iran has evoked the flawed U.S. intelligence in 2002 about Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction. Iraq had largely abandoned or frozen its nuclear, chemical and biological programs by then, but U.S. intelligence agencies told President George W. Bush’s White House that their assessment that Iraq had such weapons was ironclad.

People briefed on the new intelligence had different views on how quickly — or effectively — Iran could deploy a chemical weapon. While mounting a chemical weapon on a ballistic missile is not difficult, ensuring that the weapon can effectively disperse a chemical agent is, according to weapons experts and U.S. officials. Smuggling a bomb across a border also poses challenges.

Using a drone to deliver a chemical weapon is also a possibility.

A regional official said Israel had presented Gulf countries with claims that Iran was working to make its chemical weapons operational. Israeli officials did not share evidence but briefed the officials on their assessments, which the official said Gulf governments found unserious.

The White House did not comment, but a U.S. official said Mr. Trump would keep America and its allies safe from any potential threat. The C.I.A. declined to comment.

A spokesman for Mr. Netanyahu’s office said that “Israel closely tracks every threat posed by the Iranian terror regime and is prepared to deal with it.” A spokesman for Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return a request for comment.

While there is little debate in the U.S. intelligence community that Iran is developing chemical weapons, there is significant debate over whether its leaders would ever use those weapons, especially if not provoked by further attacks.

The U.S. director of national intelligence warned in 2024 that “Iran probably aims to continue research and development of chemical and biological agents for offensive purposes.”

Dana Stroul, the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration, said it had been known for more than two decades that Iran stockpiled components for chemical weapons but that Tehran has never deployed them.

But Iran might feel “existentially pressured and potentially crossed the line to direct offensive use of these unconventional weapons,” said Ms. Stroul, who is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

The United States has monitored a variety of threats from Iran, as intelligence collection intensified after the discovery of an Iranian plot to attack a military base in Britain used by American warplanes.

On Oct. 23, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, sent Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security adviser, a memo warning of the threat of Iranian attacks. U.S. diplomats and other personnel were then put on high alert.

U.S. agencies assess that the threat against Americans in the Middle East and several other countries is at its highest level since the war started in February, U.S. officials said.

U.S. Central Command has a plan to strike Iran beginning as early as Wednesday, after the U.S. midterm elections and when three aircraft carriers are in the region, according to U.S. officials.

The ideal conditions for the type of campaign the military has laid out will last only a short time. After early November, one of the aircraft carriers will need to return to its home port. Early November is also a period of moonless nights, the kind of deep darkness the U.S. military likes to use for its attacks.

Some Trump cabinet members have argued for more time to let a campaign of economic pressure work. They say a U.S. blockade and sanctions on the country will eventually bring down the Iranian government.

But some officials point out that Iran has been able to weather the pressure campaign and that there is little indication that the Iranian government will collapse without additional military attacks.

Stephanie Walker, a senior national security and intelligence official at the F.B.I., said last week that the Iranian threat to U.S. interests was “a top focus right now for the entirety of the U.S. government.”

Tehran’s goals, Ms. Walker said, included espionage, influence and cyberattacks. Iran-linked hackers targeted scores of water systems across the United States this summer, leading some counties to issue boil-water advisories.

Iran has also attempted to impersonate people online in order to dupe their associates into sharing access to sensitive information with them. Artificial intelligence has made this form of trickery far easier, “especially with vishing,” she said, referring to voice-based phishing attacks.

The war “changed Iran’s calculus for what they were willing to do here against us,” Ms. Walker said last week at a national security conference in Sea Island, Ga.

Reporting was contributed by Vivian Nereim and Tyler Pager in Palm Beach, Fla., Maggie Haberman in Washington and Ronen Bergman in Tel Aviv.

item.title: Trump Pushes Venezuela for Agreement Allowing U.S. Troops to Stay
item.description:
The Trump administration is negotiating an agreement with Venezuela that would lay the foundation for a potential long-term U.S. military presence in the country, U.S. officials said.

The talks could open the door to a remarkable and perhaps risky new stage in the U.S. relationship with Venezuela, as the two former adversaries attempt to move toward military cooperation.

Venezuela’s top officials have become subservient to President Trump since U.S. troops killed scores of people in a nighttime assault on Venezuela in January and took Nicolás Maduro, the country’s leader, to a prison in New York.

In a speech in Washington on Monday, Mr. Trump referred to “our conquest of Venezuela.”

The negotiations are the latest manifestation of the U.S. government’s increasingly militarized policies in Latin America. Mr. Trump and his top aides have ordered troops to carry out operations across the region, including joint actions with forces in Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela.

The U.S. military has also carried out scores of lethal strikes on civilian boats in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific that many legal experts say are extrajudicial killings.

The Trump administration has forged closer security ties with many of the region’s right-wing governments and has troops and military assets at bases across Central and South America.

Venezuela’s new authoritarian leader, Delcy Rodríguez, is an ally of Mr. Maduro and has a history of criticizing the United States, including its military. But since Mr. Maduro’s ouster, she has worked closely with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The State Department under Mr. Rubio is leading the talks on the military pact, known as a status of forces agreement, or SOFA, said the U.S. officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy.

Any details of a long-term U.S. troop presence in Venezuela, including numbers and locations, would be worked out in future agreements.

The State Department said in a statement that it has negotiated status of forces agreements with more than 100 countries. The United States maintains tens of thousands of troops on bases in some of them but only a few advisers or units in others.

The pacts, it said, “promote defense cooperation by providing a clear, predictable legal framework for U.S. forces to work on mutually agreed activities with our security partners, such as ship visits, training, exercises and humanitarian assistance.”

The Embassy of Venezuela in Washington did not reply to a request for comment.

It is extraordinary for the American government to try to reach such an arrangement with Venezuela, which recently considered the United States an enemy and which had troops killed in the U.S. assault in January.

The populist anti-American ideology in Venezuela known as Chavismo still has support among 10 to 20 percent of citizens, including in the military and security agencies, experts say. They could become vocal opponents to the negotiations.

Even outside of those ideologues, many Venezuelans bristle at what they call a new form of Western colonialism, with Mr. Trump’s boasting of taking the country’s oil. The sight of American troops in the country could fuel their anger.

State Department officials gave some congressional aides a formal briefing on the imminent negotiations with Venezuela in late October.

On Monday, Mr. Rubio met with the new foreign minister of Venezuela, Oliver Blanco, in Washington. They discussed reconciliation talks among the country’s political factions, the possibility of future elections and the potential release of political prisoners, the State Department said. Its summary of the meeting did not mention negotiations over a military agreement.

After the deadly U.S. operation on Jan. 3 in which Mr. Maduro was seized, the Pentagon said it did not have a military presence in Venezuela. When a series of devastating earthquakes hit Venezuela in June, the U.S. Southern Command sent about 2,000 troops into and around Venezuela, said the commander in charge, Gen. Francis L. Donovan. Those who entered the country have since left.

Venezuela has a coast along the Caribbean and land borders with Colombia, Brazil and Guyana, making it well suited as a regional base of operations.

The U.S. military and other American agencies are conducting operations in Colombia to try to halt drug trafficking. Smugglers move drugs from Colombia to Venezuela and then mainly to Europe.

In June, Southern Command carried out an airstrike in Venezuela that killed Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, a founder of Tren de Aragua, a criminal organization in Venezuela that the Trump administration aims to crush, officials from both countries said. The C.I.A. provided intelligence, and Venezuelan forces were involved in the operation, they said.

One question is whether the United States intends to set up and maintain American military bases in Venezuela or put troops on Venezuelan bases.

A senior State Department official said in Caracas that the United States expected to expand its security cooperation with Venezuela but asserted that any serious discussion of setting up bases was “way, way down the road.” He said there were no current talks about bases with the Venezuelan government.

The U.S. Embassy in Caracas, which recently resumed operations after being shut down for seven years, has one full-time military attaché and a handful of Marines, the official said.

The Pentagon and Southern Command’s efforts to bolster military ties in South America have focused on Ecuador and Colombia so far.

A former U.S. official who worked on military cooperation in Latin America said there were challenges to establishing a U.S. troop presence in Venezuela even if officials successfully negotiated an agreement.

One issue is the country’s shoddy infrastructure, including at the U.S. Embassy, he said. Another is the fact that the U.S. military has not engaged with Venezuelan forces in nearly a decade, so it would take some time to forge a working relationship.

The talks with Venezuela on a military agreement come at a delicate political moment because of a debate in Washington and Caracas on a timeline for elections and discussions on who might be Venezuela’s next leader.

It is the administration of Ms. Rodríguez that negotiates diplomatic agreements with the State Department. Mr. Trump has given her his full-throated support and has said Venezuela is not ready for elections.

Mr. Rubio has been nudging along political discussions within Venezuela that are supposedly aimed at making structural changes needed for fair elections. But neither he nor any Venezuelan official has given concrete dates for local or national elections.

The two governments are coming under increasing pressure to set dates, though. The most prominent Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, who has called for presidential elections by July, made a surprise return to her country in late October after being in exile for 10 months.

She made a risky, secret departure in December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway but found it impossible to travel to Venezuela earlier this year because the Trump administration had made it clear to foreign officials that it did not endorse her return, U.S. officials said.

Ms. Machado, a conservative politician, is the most viable challenger to Ms. Rodríguez for the presidency. She has criticized an oil deal that Mr. Trump and Mr. Rubio reached last year with Venezuela — and denounced Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan oilman at the center of that deal — but has not said anything about future U.S. military involvement in Venezuela.

She had supported the U.S. military’s actions in Mr. Trump’s earlier pressure campaign against Mr. Maduro.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Midterm Suspense
item.description:
And the winners are …?

Yes, you’re dying to know, and I’m dying to know — but we don’t know yet. Sometime today, though, we should have a pretty good idea whether the “blue wave” the polls have predicted has actually materialized in the U.S. midterm elections and given the Democrats control of one or both chambers of Congress, or whether Republicans will prevail.

One thing we do know already is that turnout appears to be high. American voters care about this election, a lot. Despite the efforts of some Republicans, the midterms have become all about President Trump for many voters.

We’ve collected the latest for you, as of the time this newsletter lands in your inbox. You can also follow along here for the most recent updates. (I’ll do the same!)

It has been a divisive campaign and, at times, a nasty one.

Democrats have blamed the president and his signature policies — especially tariffs and the war in Iran — for the fact that many Americans are struggling to make ends meet.

Republicans have tried to transform the election from a referendum on President Trump into a choice between their party and their Democratic opponents, whom they’ve tried to cast as far-left radicals.

Trump, for his part, has repeatedly urged his supporters to act as if his name is on the ballot, insisting that Republicans will win if his base turns out to vote.

Later today, we’ll see who prevails.

My colleague Lisa Lerer explains in the video below how voters are weighing the effects of Trump’s agenda.

What we know so far:

High turnout: The polls are still open, but many millions of votes have already been cast. In each of the major Senate battleground states, including Texas, North Carolina and Michigan, early turnout has exceeded the levels of the last midterm election.

Lots of money: These are the most expensive midterm elections, as measured in spending on political advertising, since ad tracking began in the 2018 midterms. Elon Musk alone contributed $474 million to Republican groups, candidates and their allies. That’s more than any donor has ever spent in an election cycle.

Worries about foul play: Trump has kept up a sustained attack on the integrity of U.S. elections. On Monday, he offered a $1 million reward for information that led to an election fraud conviction, without providing any details. Many election officials and Democrats worried that the offer could lead to tensions at polling stations and baseless challenges to the results. The administration has tried to prove that many noncitizens have cast ballots, but few people have been charged with offenses related to voting fraud.

Be patient: It could be days or weeks before the full results are known, particularly in races that are close. In 2024, it took three weeks to determine the winners in California’s closest House races.

Here’s more to read while we’re waiting:

A tricky task: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers are covering the midterms. They’re working to understand a large country with voters who are complicated, and sometimes contradictory. Want to read more about how our journalists are going about it? Click here.

The new swing states: Control of the Senate will hinge on the outcomes in the battleground states of Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Here’s when to expect results.

Our U.S. politics coverage is still free in The New York Times app for a limited time.

The Needle, our live forecast, returns tonight

We’ll turn on our real-time estimates of who will win the Senate and the House once enough votes have been reported.

After Israel’s election, opponents of Benjamin Netanyahu are facing a dilemma over whether Arab lawmakers should be asked to join a new government.

A Russian attack that killed at least 31 Ukrainians at a school distributing medicine and food could be among the deadliest of the entire war.

Bomb threats targeted at least seven planes in Europe. All of the flights landed safely, and officials said that no explosives had been found.

Poland beefed up security at its border with Russia in response to what it called “disturbing movement” that could be preparations for “armed incursions.”

On a Caribbean tour, King Charles expressed “profound personal sorrow” and “horror” over Britain’s role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade.

Ian Berry, the only photographer who documented the 1960 Sharpeville massacre, a turning point in the struggle against apartheid in South Africa, died at 92.

item.title: On Cusp of Renewed War, More Iranians Are Calling for Nuclear Weapons
item.description:
From pulpits at Friday prayers to street rallies, Iranian clerics and officials are increasingly urging the country’s leaders to reverse their longtime pledge not to pursue nuclear weapons.

This demand, once seen as a fringe position held by hard-liners, is moving into mainstream public debate, and the shift could have dramatic consequences for Iran, whose government has for decades argued that its nuclear program was solely for peaceful purposes.

“We must be equipped with nuclear weapons — so that we can fight the criminal America with strength, God willing,” Ali Sepahvand, the Friday prayer leader in Iran’s western city of Kuhdasht, said last week, according to a widely distributed video.

As his voice echoed through a prayer hall, covered in photographs of commanders killed in the war with the United States and Israel this past year, the congregants chanted: “Nuclear deterrence is our inalienable right!”

The growing calls for Iran to pursue nuclear weapons come as the country’s leaders engage in diplomatic efforts to stave off renewed war with the United States and Israel, an outcome widely considered likely after the American midterm elections on Tuesday.

For decades, Iran’s officials have publicly endorsed the fatwa, or religious edict, from its supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, which forbade the development and use of nuclear weapons. Issued in his capacity as the head of Iran’s theocratic state, his decree barred Iranian institutions, including the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, from pursuing a nuclear bomb.

Yet at the same time, Western intelligence agencies in past years reported signs Iran was enriching uranium to levels close to those that could be used to develop a bomb. Some officials in Israel and the United States accused Iran of preparing to build one, regardless of the fatwa.

To curb this threat, the United States and other world powers reached an agreement with Iran in 2015 to restrict its nuclear activities. Three years later, President Trump pulled out of that agreement.

Ayatollah Khamenei’s strategy, regional analysts say, had been to keep Iran’s nuclear intentions ambiguous in hopes of deterring attacks on Iran without it actually becoming a nuclear power.

But that approach failed to prevent the two wars Israel and the United States have waged against Iran since June 2025 — including the one in which Mr. Khamenei was himself killed in February.

“He created this neither in nor out situation, where they paid for a bomb they didn’t have,” said Mohammad Ali Shabani, an Iran analyst who edits the independent regional news site Amwaj.media. “Now, there is this sense that unless you have this ultimate weapon, you could end up at the mercy of not just the U.S., but Israel, at any point.”

President Trump’s own comments may strengthen this assessment, analysts say.

“If they had a nuclear weapon, I’d be calling the Supreme Leader and I’d be saying, ‘Mr. Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’ As opposed to bombing the crap out of him,” Mr. Trump said at the Republican midterm convention in September.

Inside Iran, calls for withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, or N.P.T., which prohibits development of a nuclear weapon, have been growing ever since Israel and the United States attacked in 2025.

In recent weeks, an increasing number of Iranian political and religious figures have added their voices to this chorus, suggesting to some Iran analysts that there is an effort orchestrated, or at least enabled, by the country’s leadership.

It is unclear whether serious debate over Iran’s nuclear doctrine has reached the new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei. But on Saturday, Iran’s top national security figure, Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview on state television that Iran’s leaders were discussing it.

“No new decision has been made yet,” he said. “Of course, the debate now is whether we want to keep the same doctrine we had before the war, if war breaks out again.”

Advocating for withdrawal from the N.P.T. was once a minority position within Iran’s leadership, said Mohammad Ghaderi, a foreign affairs expert in Tehran.

Now, he argued, it is becoming a majority view. “They argue that if the military threats from the United States and Israel persist, withdrawing from the N.P.T. represents a crucial step toward establishing deterrence,” he said.

Raising the nuclear prospect at a time when Iran could be at the cusp of another possible attack by the United States or Israel may itself be a strategy, said Omid Memarian, an Iran analyst at DAWN, a Washington-based Middle East research group.

Mr. Rezaei’s entry into the debate, while Qatar has been leading intensive mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran, may be an attempt to push the United States to reach a deal, Mr. Memarian said.

“They are playing with this card: If the negotiation fails, we will seek a different path, and it will be costly for you,” he said.

Especially notable has been the number of Friday prayer leaders adding their voices to the calls and effectively challenging the late ayatollah’s fatwa.

“The taboo is gone,” said Mr. Shabani. “A religious foundation for the shift is here. The question is whether a strategic or political shift will follow.”

Some of Iran’s leading reformist figures, like the president Masoud Pezeshkian and former president Hassan Rouhani, continue to back Iran’s peaceful nuclear doctrine.

In Iran’s leading reformist newspaper, Shargh, a former diplomat, Kourosh Ahmadi, warned this week that abandoning that doctrine poses grave risks. The plethora of pro-weapon statements from prominent figures, he said, “is dangerous because it makes the work of officials trying to prevent another war more difficult.”

And until Iran could manage to build a bomb, he argued, the chances of being attacked would actually increase.

After U.S. and Israeli strikes wiped out most of Iran’s top leadership and battered its infrastructure, it is harder for critics of the nuclear option to make their case, said Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy, a Washington-based think tank.

“The central problem for advocates of restraint is explaining what Iran gained from remaining below the nuclear threshold,” he said.

At the same time, he said, a new round of U.S. attacks “could strengthen the very arguments for the nuclear weapons that Washington says it wants to prevent.”

At public prayers in Tehran on Friday, the prayer leader, Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, declared that changing Iran’s nuclear doctrine was “a national demand,” according to a video posted on social media.

His congregants immediately responded with a refrain common at government-sponsored rallies from decades past: “Nuclear energy is our inalienable right!”

“This is an old slogan,” he told them, and smiled: “We have gone way beyond that.”

Leily Nikounazar and Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting

item.title: U.S. Assisted Venezuela in Deadly Drone Strike, Officials Say
item.description:
For years, a Colombian rebel army operated freely across the border in Venezuela, allowed to traffic cocaine and oversee illicit gold mines under Nicolás Maduro, the country’s former president.

But with Mr. Maduro forcibly removed by the United States and Venezuela’s government under the thumb of the Trump administration, Venezuela’s military last week launched a deadly attack on the group, the National Liberation Army, better known by its Spanish initials, ELN.

The attack, according to four U.S. officials, was carried out on Friday with the help of U.S. intelligence and drones. It was not previously public who had been responsible for the attack.

The joint operation underscores how the Trump administration is increasingly enmeshed in Venezuela’s domestic affairs and how it has embraced a militarized strategy to combat drug trafficking in Latin America.

The attack was not the first joint operation in the country. In June, a strike by the United States and Venezuela killed a leader of Tren de Aragua, the transnational gang.

The New York Times reported this week that the Trump administration is aiming to establish a long-term U.S. military presence in Venezuela.

A Venezuelan human rights organization, Fundaredes, first alerted the public to Friday’s attack, which took place in the Apure region near the Colombian border, after organizers spoke with survivors and local residents.

At least 23 people were killed and many more injured, the group said, after drones bombed an ELN site that was a known hub for cocaine distribution.

The U.S. officials who confirmed details of the attack requested anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter.

For years, the ELN operated freely in Venezuela, viewing the country as a refuge from military attacks in Colombia and a prime location for flying cocaine smuggled from Colombia to other countries. The Venezuelan government was seen as its ally.

On a visit to Colombia in September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the ELN could no longer be allowed to operate “with impunity” in Venezuela, and that the topic had been raised with the interim government of Delcy Rodríguez.

“We have to confront it,” he said.

While it was not clear who piloted the drones used in Friday’s attack, the type of drone involved is typically operated by U.S. forces, one of the U.S. officials said.

The State Department referred questions about the attack to the Department of Defense, which said questions should be directed to Venezuela’s government. Venezuelan officials did not respond to a request for comment.

On Monday, a senior Venezuelan military official confirmed that the country’s armed forces had carried out the attack on the ELN in Apures. The official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, asked not to be named. The person had not been personally briefed on the U.S. role.

Representatives of the ELN did not respond to requests for comment.

Juan Francisco García, the Fundaredes coordinator for the Apures region, said residents who lived on ranches near the site of the attack had described hearing two large explosions on Friday morning. They approached and found bodies scattered around the bombed site, which Mr. García, who works in the area, said was known to be used by the ELN for shipping cocaine.

Security analysts say the ELN had consolidated control of much of the Venezuelan border and used air strips there to ship Colombian cocaine by plane to other countries in Latin America, including Mexico.

Mr. García shared photos and videos with The Times he said were taken by residents on Friday. One photo shows, from a distance, a helicopter and several smaller, dark shapes hovering over pastureland. A video shows bodies amid debris.

Mr. García, who said he visited a nearby morgue and saw several victims’ bodies over the weekend, said that many of the corpses had been “mutilated” by explosives.

He said that interviews with survivors of the attack, and relatives of victims, had indicated that not all the victims were fighters.

Those killed included pilots, goods suppliers and the relatives or partners of ELN members, he said. One was a woman in her 60s whom he described as the wife of a pilot.

The ELN is known to recruit members from poor communities where there are few employment opportunities. In areas where the group is the de facto authority, locals say they often feel they have to cooperate.

Mr. García noted that, while less than half of the victims had been identified by Monday, government IDs found on some bodies showed that the victims were Venezuelan, not Colombian.

Since no government officially took responsibility for the attack, theories have swirled in recent days about who was responsible and whether any group leader had been killed.

The attack came on the heels of several bombings against ELN targets in Colombia ordered by the country’s conservative new president, Abelardo De La Espriella, who has vowed to crush armed groups that do not surrender.

After the ELN released a video in September in which a well-known commander defied the new president and said the group would keep fighting, Mr. De La Espriella responded by calling the ELN commander, known as Silvana Guerrero, a “terrorist” who would end up in a body bag.

On Friday, the day of the attack in Venezuela, Colombia’s armed forces reportedly dropped fliers over the border city of Cúcuta offering reward money for the ELN’s top commanders.

Colombian defense officials denied playing any role in the operation in Venezuela.

Security analysts said the military strategy against the ELN — which is said to have around 6,000 fighters — now appears to be to squeeze the group on both sides of the border at once so that it does not have a place to hide.

The attack comes as the Trump administration has designated around two dozen criminal groups in Latin America as terrorist organizations and is launching a military plan to crush Latin America’s “narcoterrorists.” It has also put pressure on leaders to target trafficking groups and to capture or kill group leaders.

Though legal experts say the terrorist label does not confer the authority to use lethal force as a first resort, the label has, nonetheless, been frequently invoked by top Trump administration officials when publicizing military strikes against accused traffickers, including boat strikes that so far have killed 244 people.

“The United States military will treat these organizations like the terrorists they are,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said after a lethal strike last October on a boat allegedly linked to the ELN. “They will be hunted and killed, just like Al Qaeda.”

Formed in rural Colombia in the 1960s, the ELN merged Marxism with Roman Catholic liberation theology. It later resorted to violent tactics like kidnapping and drug trafficking, and in 1997 it was among the first groups to be placed on the State Department list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

The ELN suffered severe setbacks amid a major U.S.-backed military offensive two decades ago, but survived and outlasted other Colombian groups that laid down arms in peace deals.

Analysts say a significant reason for its survival was its ability to seek refuge and expand its territorial control into Venezuela.

U.S. officials have accused the Maduro regime, including Diosdado Cabello, the powerful interior minister, of allowing the group to seize control of large areas along the border. Residents say the state largely overlooked the effects of its illegal activities, including gold mining, on the environment and everyday people.

Venezuelan officials were said to have profited from these activities. The United Nations has long cited reports of the Venezuelan military and ELN fighters working together to smuggle gold.

The United States, in its criminal indictment against Mr. Maduro, also claimed that the former Venezuelan leader and Mr. Cabello partnered with the ELN to send cocaine to the United States.

The ELN also operated as an extension of the Venezuelan military, confronting other criminal groups and enforcing state interests, according to International Crisis Group, an independent organization that has done fieldwork on the border.

As Venezuela became more isolated — and economically desperate — the ELN also filled the vacuum left by the state, providing Venezuelans with work, services and even basic goods.

The Venezuelan military official who said Venezuelan armed forces had carried out Friday’s attack, noted that only after Mr. Maduro had been removed were military units encouraged to attack the ELN.

Anatoly Kurmanaev, Simón Posada and Federico Rios contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: How Will Tonight Go? Here Are Races That Will Provide Early Clues.
item.description:
On Election Day, states where polls close and ballot counting begins early could offer the first concrete clues for how the rest of the night will go, with control of Congress on the line.

Here are some poll closures to watch in the first hours of election night. All times are Eastern.

President Trump won Kentucky’s Sixth Congressional District by 15 points in 2024, but its House race this year has been rated a tossup by nonpartisan election forecasters. If the Democratic candidate, Zach Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy veteran, beats the Republican, Dr. Ralph Alvarado, a physician and former state senator endorsed by Mr. Trump, it would signal Democrats’ strength overall.

In Indiana’s traditionally conservative Fifth District, Representative Victoria Spartz, a Republican, won by about 19 points in 2024 and is favored to retain the seat on Tuesday, according to forecasters. But her lead has narrowed the area, where Democrats are usually not competitive. If the winner is her Democratic challenger, State Senator J.D. Ford, it could signal broader Democratic victories.

Democrats do not usually win votes from rural white voters in either district, and if one or both Democratic candidates prevail, that “would indicate that we are winning in a way that is going to translate across the country in many similar districts,” said CJ Warnke, a spokesman for the House Majority PAC, the biggest super PAC for House Democrats.

If a Republican wins either race, it could mean that their party might mitigate its losses elsewhere.

Democrats have clear edge in Senate and House

Democrats running for Senate are performing well in Republican strongholds like South Carolina and Texas.

Very likely Dem.

>95% chance of control

Very likely Dem.

>95% chance of control

Republican state lawmakers redrew several congressional districts to favor their party. Despite that, analysts say many of these districts have close races. If Democrats win in the Seventh, Ninth, 14th, 22nd or 25th Districts, it could bode well for them elsewhere.

Republican victories in these districts could mean that the party’s redistricting efforts successfully blocked a Democratic surge during a difficult year for Republicans.

Republicans are favored to win the Senate and governor’s races in Florida, according to analysts. But Democrats have lately been hopeful about the governor’s race, where David Jolly, the Democratic nominee, is challenging Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican. If Democrats win the Senate and governor’s races, they are having a very good night.

Even if there is a victory for Mr. Donalds or the Republican incumbent in the Senate, Ashley Moody, Democrats may find that some demographic groups bear watching.

South Carolina’s First District has not only been traditionally conservative-leaning, but it has also been gerrymandered by Republicans to further benefit their party. Still, the race has been rated a tossup by analysts.

If Nancy Lacore, a Democratic former Navy admiral who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, wins the open seat over Jenny Costa Honeycutt, a Republican local councilwoman and lawyer, it would signal that a strong Democratic candidate could win in red territory elsewhere in the country. But if Ms. Honeycutt wins, it could reflect the strength of the region’s conservative base and the redrawn district lines.

The chances of a Democratic victory in the state’s Senate race are slimmer, but the lead held by Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, has narrowed throughout her campaign. If she loses to Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician running as a Democrat, that could mean that Republicans may lose their majority in the upper chamber.

Virginia’s Second District traditionally swings, and analysts said that the Democratic candidate, former Representative Elaine Luria, was favored to flip it. The result could indicate whether a strong Republican candidate like Jen Kiggans, a two-term incumbent, can survive Democratic momentum.

Mr. Trump won the neighboring First District by five points in 2024, but analysts said the House race there this year was a tossup. If Shannon Taylor, a Democratic prosecutor, defeats Representative Rob Wittman, a Republican first elected in 2007, Democrats could be in for a great night.

item.title: Spain’s Transport Minister Resigns After Deadly High-Speed Rail Crash
item.description:
Spain’s transport minister announced his resignation on Tuesday evening, nearly a week after the deadliest train crash in a decade killed nearly 70 people and raised doubts about the country’s once-vaunted rail system ahead of national elections.

“A transport minister cannot remain in office after two accidents of such severity in less than a year,” the minister, Óscar Puente, told lawmakers on Tuesday evening after days of resisting calls for his resignation.

Mr. Puente’s resignation came at the end of a bruising day of questioning for the minister, who gave lawmakers a detailed account of the events leading to the accident, in which one high-speed train rear-ended another on the same tracks.

“You’re so good at explaining why people die on trains, and so bad at preventing them from dying on trains,” said Ester Muñoz, the spokeswoman for the main opposition conservative party, the Popular Party.

Mr. Puente’s resignation reflected his increasingly untenable position ahead of snap elections on Nov. 29 and suggested that he had become a liability to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who had stood by him. Many political parties had demanded his resignation, and recent polls showed that a majority of Spaniards believed Mr. Puente should step down.

“Óscar Puente has faced up to his responsibilities, offered solutions and then stepped aside,” Mr. Sánchez said on social media after the minister’s resignation. He added, “Politicians like him bring dignity to our country.”

The crash shook Spaniards’ confidence in their high-speed railway system, long considered the jewel of a modernizing country that had shown it was on par with the rest of Europe. But in January, a crash on the same line between Madrid and Seville killed 46 people, and another 69 died in the collision last week.

After the crashes, analysts said, Spaniards increasingly felt that the country’s infrastructure was not working and was unsafe, a view that could damage Mr. Sánchez politically as his party already trails in the polls.

Mr. Puente’s reputation as an attack dog for the government, known for lashing out at political rivals on social media, only increased the calls for his resignation.

Mr. Puente began his parliamentary hearing at 5 p.m. with a lengthy explanation of how the crash happened, faulting the errors of rail traffic controllers in Madrid, who had taken over after an automatic safety system went down in the area near Toledo, in central Spain. The controllers authorized a train to proceed at high speed though another was stalled in front of it, he said.

Mr. Puente also announced a battery of measures and new protocols to improve railway safety. But lawmakers across the political spectrum held him responsible for the accidents on his watch and demanded his resignation.

Ms. Muñoz of the Popular Party said it was “incomprehensible” that two deadly tragedies had occurred on the same rail line. “This is not an isolated failure; it is a systemic failure,” she said.

Pepa Millán, a lawmaker from the far-right party Vox, asked Mr. Puente whether he could “sleep soundly?”

But even coalition partners in the left-wing government asked him to step down, and Mr. Puente framed his resignation as a necessity.

“It is a matter of political dignity, consistency,” he said, “and empathy for the victims.”

item.title: Helicopters Collide Over Everest Trail, Killing 1 and Injuring 3 Others
item.description:
A midair collision of two helicopters near Mount Everest on Tuesday left one Indian tourist dead and a visitor from New Zealand and two pilots injured, according to Nepal’s civil aviation authority.

The helicopters collided as they were attempting to land in the Pheriche area of the Solukhumbu district of Nepal around 8 in the morning, the aviation authority said in a statement. Pheriche is a village at an altitude of about 13,900 feet along the Everest Base Camp trekking route.

Video of the accident showed that, in apparently clear weather, the propellers of a lower helicopter made contact with a second aircraft that had been flying higher nearby and swooped downward rapidly. Both helicopters fell to the ground not far apart and appeared to have been destroyed in the collision.

The crash cast a pall on the popular tourist destination during the autumn climbing season and highlighted the dangers that some locals and government officials have warned of as flights in the region have proliferated.

The Nepali authorities identified the dead tourist as Vasanth Kumar Balaramaramadu, 44, of India and the injured visitor, who was being treated at a hospital in Kathmandu, as Shailesh Kisan Patel of New Zealand. The aviation authority’s statement expressed hope for a speedy recovery for the injured, including two unnamed pilots.

In a post, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu expressed “its deepest condolences on the unfortunate demise of an Indian national” and said it was working “in close coordination with Nepali authorities for early repatriation of the mortal remains of the deceased.”

The aviation authority in Nepal said it was investigating the collision and would take any actions or corrective measures needed to address potential issues. “Preliminary reports suggest miscommunication between the pilots, as the area is outside the coverage of Lukla Airport’s air traffic control tower and pilots have to communicate with each other,” Mukesh Dangol, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, told The Kathmandu Post.

The perils of heavy helicopter traffic in the mountainous region are well known, and the Nepali government has struggled to strike a balance between the needs of a thriving tourism industry and the demand for better regulation to ensure safety and preservation of the natural environment.

In 2023, five visitors from Mexico and a Nepali pilot were killed when their helicopter crashed during a sightseeing trip over Mount Everest.

Local officials and those at the Sagarmatha National Park, home to Mount Everest, have clashed with government regulators over helicopter restrictions in recent years. In 2024, the park authorities said they would begin restricting helicopter sightseeing tours and some other flights in 2025, a rule that civil aviation regulators initially said the park had no authority to enforce.

item.title: Anthrax Outbreak in Africa’s Oldest National Park Is Killing Hippos
item.description:
An anthrax outbreak in a park in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been killing hippopotamuses, threatening vulnerable wildlife and raising concerns about human exposure to the disease.

The outbreak at Virunga National Park — Africa’s oldest national park — has killed 30 hippopotamuses since September, when observers first started noticing suspicious carcasses, Laura Parker, who leads the park’s conservation programs, said in an email on Tuesday. The cause of the animals’ deaths, and the outbreak, has since been confirmed by laboratory analyses, she noted.

This is the second outbreak of anthrax in the park since last year, and it comes as Congo is contending with an Ebola epidemic that has killed more than 4,800 people since May and strained the country’s resources.

Doctors who have analyzed anthrax outbreaks in the region say that the disease represents a significant public health challenge, intersecting with issues like food insecurity, conflict and poverty, and disproportionately affecting rural populations with limited access to health care.

Park officials have been raising awareness among local communities to ensure people do not touch or consume meat from any affected carcasses and report any such finds to the authorities, Ms. Parker said.

“Virunga’s response is focused on surveillance, safe carcass management and reducing risks to both wildlife and people. Teams are monitoring the affected area, documenting new mortalities and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses,” she said.

Anthrax is a zoonotic disease caused by a bacterium found naturally in soil around the world. It often affects livestock and wild animals that can become infected when they breathe in, eat or drink spores in contaminated soil, plants or water. The spores can lie dormant in soil for years or decades, so outbreaks recur in areas where they are already in the environment, as in the national park.

Last year’s anthrax outbreak killed about 65 hippos in the park and affected people in the region. Human exposure to anthrax is most commonly linked to contact with infected animals, and community outreach is vital to preventing deaths or illness in people, public health experts say.

Anthrax outbreaks are linked to unusual climatic conditions, including prolonged dry periods, and a lack of rain may be to blame for the latest episodes of the disease, park officials surmise. There has been significant rainfall of late and no new cases confirmed in two weeks, so they are cautiously optimistic, but monitoring protocols continue, Ms. Parker said.

Virunga National Park is recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site for its exceptional wildlife and biodiversity. It was established in 1925. While rich in natural resources, however, the park is in one of the world’s poorest countries, one that has been plagued by decades of conflict.

On its website, the park is described as being located “in a region which has been deeply impacted by the effects of war and armed conflict for over 20 years.” Conflict and poverty are among the forces driving wildlife poaching in Congo, with hippos poached for their meat by armed groups and impoverished people, as well as for the ivory in their teeth.

The park, which had about 29,000 hippos 50 years ago, saw much of the population depleted over the years. This year, it reported about 2,700 hippos, noting that the latest figures suggested efforts to protect the vulnerable animals, including by having more rangers patrolling the park, were leading to a slow recovery.

The latest anthrax outbreak has dealt a blow to the project.

item.title: U.K. Supreme Court to Hear Challenge to Ban on Palestine Action: What to Know
item.description:
Britain’s decision to outlaw Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian direct-action group, as a terrorist organization has been challenged in a succession of legal hearings since it was imposed last year. Now, the country’s Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge against the ban and decide its future.

The British government accused Palestine Action of orchestrating “a nationwide campaign of direct criminal action,” putting national security at risk. According to the government’s independent adviser on counterterrorism legislation, it was the first time a protest group that did not call for violence against people was proscribed under counterterrorism laws.

Here’s what to know.

Palestine Action was founded in 2020 as a pro-Palestinian protest group that largely focuses its efforts on demonstrations against corporate and military targets linked to the sale and export of defense equipment to Israel. The group says it does not promote violence against individuals.

It was co-founded by Huda Ammori, an advocate who had previously worked for a Palestinian rights organization, and Richard Barnard, an activist linked with other grass roots movements, including Extinction Rebellion, a global environmental group.

During legal proceedings challenging the ban, Britain’s High Court said that the group claimed to have a mailing list of some 20,000 people but that the “extent and nature” of Palestine Action’s membership and organization was “largely unexplained.” Analysts said that before it was disbanded, Palestine Action was run by a relatively small, committed group of activists.

The group’s actions have drawn international attention. President Trump criticized it after activists were accused of vandalizing one of his Scottish golf resorts by defacing the clubhouse and spraying “Gaza is not 4 sale” across a green. Mr. Trump called the demonstrators “terrorists” and said he hoped they would be “treated harshly.”

The Terrorism Act 2000, introduced under a previous Labour prime minister, Tony Blair, allows the government to ban any group “concerned in terrorism.” It contains a broad definition of terrorism that includes damage to property, not just people, if it is carried out for ideological reasons.

The British government announced its plan to designate Palestine Action a terrorist group in June 2025, three days after some of its members damaged military planes using red paint at Britain’s largest air force base, at Brize Norton in Oxfordshire. Yvette Cooper, then the home secretary, said the group’s activities met the legal definition of terrorism because they included “serious damage to property.”

The ban was imposed in July, and the group was added to the statutory list of more than 80 banned terrorist organizations, alongside the Islamic State, Al Qaeda, and Atomwaffen Division, a white supremacist group. At the time, Palestine Action said it was “plainly preposterous” to group it with such organizations.

The ban made it a criminal offense to belong to Palestine Action, express an opinion or belief in support of the group, or wear clothing or carry items that “arouse reasonable suspicion that the individual is a member or supporter” of the group, among other actions. The maximum penalty for belonging to or expressing support for the group is 14 years in prison.

In August, the United States followed suit, designating Palestine Action as a terrorist group.

More than 4,000 people had been arrested across Britain for showing support for the group as of Nov. 1, according to Defend Our Juries, a civil liberties group. Between Sept. 11, 2001, and March 31, 2025, there were a total of 5,734 terrorism arrests in Britain.

The arrests related to Palestine Action stemmed largely from coordinated demonstrations, analysts say, where some protesters have deliberately risked detention by holding placards reading: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Hundreds of people were detained over the weekend outside the U.S. Embassy in London after staging such a protest.

Some civil liberties organizations argue that using counterterrorism legislation against Palestine Action is overreach and part of a wider crackdown on protest in Britain. They contend that existing criminal laws cover property destruction, whereas proscription criminalizes anyone expressing moral support for the proscribed group, including by attending peaceful gatherings.

In July 2025, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, called the move a “disproportionate and unnecessary” expansion of counterterrorism powers and called on the British government to rescind its decision.

In written submissions to the Supreme Court, Amnesty International and Liberty argue that the proscription of Palestine Action has silenced broad segments of civil society, academics, journalists and even their own human rights organizations.

David Mead, a human rights law scholar at the University of East Anglia, said the central legal dispute turns on whether the ban is proportionate.

“The surprising thing is the U.K. state’s seeming need to use terrorism legislation on a group such as this,” Professor Mead said.

Ms. Ammori, the co-founder, first challenged the ban in June 2025, and the case has since wound its way through the legal system. In February, the High Court ruled the ban unlawful, calling it disproportionate and an infringement on fundamental rights to free expression and assembly.

That decision was overturned in June by the Court of Appeal. Ms. Ammori appealed that ruling, sending the case to the Supreme Court for what will be the final word in British domestic courts.

Supreme Court rulings are usually issued in three to six months, but legal analysts said the court could rule sooner in this case as hundreds of people arrested and charged in relation to protests are awaiting trial.

Ms. Ammori has said that if the Supreme Court upholds the ban, she plans to take the case to the European Court of Human Rights.

Stephen Castle, Lizzie Dearden and Michael Shear contributed to this report
