item.title: Australian Court Hears Challenge to Social Media Ban
item.description:
The High Court of Australia began hearing arguments on Tuesday in two legal challenges to a law barring people younger than 16 from social media, in cases that may determine the fate of a ban that was closely watched and replicated around the world.

Over two days, the court will consider cases brought by an Australian digital rights advocacy group and the U.S.-based discussion platform Reddit. Both plaintiffs contend that the law infringes on young people’s right to political participation by restricting free speech and access to information.

The law, which took effect in December, was hailed as a world-first attempt to counter the harms of algorithm-driven social media content on developing brains. There were early indications that a majority of Australian teenagers who had been using social media before the ban have continued to access it; but a growing list of countries have nevertheless passed similar measures.

Reddit is one of 10 companies covered by the Australian law, which also requires that Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube install age restrictions.

In the court cases, the Digital Freedom Project and Reddit argued that the law was unconstitutional because it violated the implied political rights of 13- to 15-year-olds. The Digital Freedom Project, headed by a libertarian state legislator, sued to block the law shortly before it took effect, while Reddit filed its challenge two days after it came into force. The cases are being jointly heard by the court in Australia’s capital, Canberra.

In its filings, lawyers for the Digital Freedom Project said that social media platforms provide “fora for political communication.” Young Australians would receive information, express views, engage in discussions, pose questions to elected officials and organize political action through social media, they argued.

They noted that 15-year-olds are prospective electors who will reach the legal voting age within Australia’s three-year federal election cycle and should be allowed to participate in political debates and exchanges.

Reddit also contended that the law violates the “implied freedom” of political communication guaranteed by Australia’s Constitution. Because young people disproportionately get their news from social media, the law interferes with their ability to participate in the political process, its lawyers argued.

They pointed out that the eSafety commissioner, the head of the regulatory agency tasked with implementing and enforcing the law, has said in media interviews that the legislation is a “blunt force approach” and with “very thin scaffolding.”

In response, the government argued in its filings that the restriction was necessary to protect children from design features that encourage addictive use. Social media use may also affect brain development; have negative effects on sleep; or result in mental health consequences like depression, anxiety or disordered eating, it argued.

The risks to young people are baked into the design of the 10 platforms, including algorithmic recommendations, infinite scroll, notifications, alerts and likes, the government’s lawyers wrote.

The ban put the burden on companies to keep children from holding accounts on their services, with the threat of a fine of up to about 99 million Australian dollars, or about $70 million. The eSafety Commission has said that it has opened investigations into five of the platforms for noncompliance.

It is unclear when the court will issue decisions.

The addictive features have been at the heart of a string of personal injury lawsuits in U.S. courts against the tech giants. In August, Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, reached a landmark settlement with 47 U.S. states and other jurisdictions, agreeing to pay up to $17.1 billion and make major changes to its products.

item.title: A Test for Israeli Democracy: Should Jews Ask Arabs to Join the Government?
item.description:
Israel’s democracy is facing a huge test after Arab political parties made historic gains in last week’s election.

And opponents of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are facing an enormous dilemma over whether Arab lawmakers should now be given a share of power in a new government.

Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents secured a clear majority in the Parliament by winning 67 out of 120 seats. But 19 of these were won by the Arab parties, and their inclusion in a governing coalition is seen as so problematic by many Israeli Jews that opposition leaders are putting themselves through contortions looking for ways to form a government that would not rely on Arab lawmakers.

The aversion to building a government with the two main Arab factions — the United Arab List, or Raam, and the Joint List, which comprises three smaller parties — is enormously frustrating to political activists who helped drive Arab turnout to a near-record high of 77 percent last week.

“Why is it so complicated? A vote of an Arab citizen of Israel should equal no less than the vote of a Jewish citizen,” said Alon-Lee Green, a founder of the Jewish-Arab organization Standing Together.

The efforts to sideline the Arab parties also fuel complaints among many Arab citizens, who represent about 20 percent of the country’s population, that Israeli Jews welcome their participation in the political process only up to the point where they might wield real power.

“This is the problem with Israeli democracy,” said Thabet Abu Rass, a longtime advocate for Arab-Jewish partnership. “It’s a democracy for Jews, but it’s a Jewish state for Arab citizens like me. We Arab citizens are entitled to the same rights, and would like to use them to dictate who’s going to lead the country.”

“But some Jews say no, democracy is for Jews only,” he said. This has become especially true since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, he said.

Indeed, welcoming the Arab parties into a new government, particularly at a time of conflict, is dismissed by many Jewish Israelis as unworkable, overly risky, and even unconscionable.

Few would deny that racism plays a part. But Israeli Jews also view the particular Arab parties — Raam, headed by Mansour Abbas, and the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen — with varying degrees of skepticism.

Mr. Abbas’s party has its roots in the Muslim Brotherhood movement, as does Hamas, a history that right-wing critics often highlight in denouncing him.

But Mr. Abbas was once the first lawmaker from an independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, and he has won many Jewish admirers by working with Jewish lawmakers. He has focused on domestic issues affecting Arab citizens, like violent crime and discriminatory housing policies, and devoted little attention to Israel’s policies in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

The Joint List’s members, by contrast, have focused more on Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in the occupied territories and have generally preferred to criticize government policy from the opposition. Some have denounced Israeli military actions, assailed Israel’s war in Gaza as genocide or referred to slain Palestinian militants as “martyrs.”

“Abbas managed to make himself more legitimate because he made it very clear he’s in politics to look after the domestic affairs of his own community,” said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group. “But you don’t hear the same music from the members of the Joint List.”

Mr. Plesner noted that even Mr. Abbas, when asked whether he supports toppling Hamas, deflects the question. “Any Zionist Israeli expects that any government would work toward toppling Hamas, because of what Hamas did and wants to do to Israel,” Mr. Plesner said.

Mr. Abbas and Mr. Jabareen bristle at such questions as demeaning and tantamount to demanding loyalty oaths. Both men have condemned the Oct. 7 attack, and Mr. Abbas has said that such violence has only harmed the Palestinian cause.

Before last week’s election, Arab parties never held more than 15 seats in Parliament. Until Mr. Abbas joined the governing coalition in 2021, Arab party leaders generally resisted taking part in governments and thus sharing in responsibility for Israel’s occupation and military actions.

But discriminatory policies, like the demolition of Arab citizens’ homes built without official permits, and soaring crime in Arab towns that Arab Israelis attribute to police negligence, have prodded lawmakers like Mr. Jabareen and others in the Joint List to vow to do all they can to drive Mr. Netanyahu’s government from power.

Discrimination against Arab citizens also undercuts Israel when it trumpets its democratic credentials beyond its borders.

For the anti-Netanyahu opposition, led by the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, the options for assembling a governing coalition are all uncomfortable.

He could try forming a minority government of fewer than 61 seats in which one or both of the Arab parties would be left outside the coalition but would cooperate to some degree, opposing no-confidence votes in Parliament. Or he could agree to a unity government, if Mr. Netanyahu or some of his allies were to accept the opposition’s terms to share power.

Mr. Eisenkot could also accept a new round of elections in hopes of a better result, though many in the opposition fear this would benefit Mr. Netanyahu, whose alliance netted only 53 seats in the balloting last week.

Rula Daood, another leader of Standing Together, said that by shying away from including Arab parties in a new government, Mr. Eisenkot was playing into Mr. Netanyahu’s hands. She accused the prime minister of seeking to delegitimize the Arab vote by claiming, without evidence, that Arab parties stole the election.

Zvi Hauser, a former center-right lawmaker, warned in the newspaper Israel Hayom that bringing the Arab parties into government could cause a catastrophe. Coalition members, he said, would hold “worldviews that disagree even on basic questions of national security.”

Mr. Hauser wrote that every vote on policies affecting Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, enforcement of housing rules in Arab communities or the demolition of the homes of those who attack Israelis could become “a test of coalition survival.”

Yossi Klein Halevi, an author and senior fellow at the Shalom Hartman Institute in Jerusalem, said that he was crestfallen last week when Mr. Abbas, whom he admired, sidestepped a television interviewer’s challenge that he label Hamas a terrorist organization.

Mr. Halevi has denounced Mr. Netanyahu for dividing the Israeli mainstream into his coalition — which puts a priority on Israel’s Jewish nature — and an opposition that prioritizes Israel’s democratic values. But Mr. Halevi said he feared that if Mr. Eisenkot formed a government relying on the two Arab parties, it would destroy the possibility of repairing that rupture for a generation.

“We will be seen as preferring anti-Zionists to our fellow Jews,” he said. “And that will be seen very widely by Jews on the right, and even some in the center, as a betrayal of the most basic Jewish solidarity.”

Among Mr. Eisenkot’s allies, Yair Golan of the left-wing Democrats party has spoken most enthusiastically of Arab party support. In an interview, he said Israel needed to cure itself of the “psychosis” of treating Arab citizens as potential traitors or second-class citizens, arguing that the Arab public had overwhelmingly proved its loyalty and solidarity since Oct. 7.

“They are a part of us,” he said. “We are on the same team.”

Mr. Golan, a former deputy chief of staff in the Israeli military, also dismissed the idea that it was risky to national security to include Arab lawmakers in the cabinet, saying that they would be excluded from the smaller security cabinet where operational decisions are made.

Mr. Golan said he envisioned a government including Raam and relying on outside support from the Joint List. He compared this to the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in the 1990s, which led effectively with just 56 seats in Parliament and outside Arab backing.

Some Israelis say the election results have presented Israel with a golden opportunity. By making common cause with Arab lawmakers, they say, the opposition could finally establish a national commission of inquiry into the security failures that led up to the Oct. 7 attacks and adopt military conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, who have long been exempt.

“It’s the most delicious moment,” said Yosef Abramowitz, a Jewish renewable-energy entrepreneur who said he had voted for Raam.

“Everybody has to grow up — now,” he said. “The Arabs have to break free of the Palestinian narrative as their organizing thesis. And Israeli Jewish society has to say that a national commission of inquiry and a full military draft are more important than the mythology that all Arabs are terrorists and terror supporters.”

item.title: The Iran War Is Unpopular. Trump Keeps Talking About It Anyway.
item.description:
The war in Iran is deeply unpopular with Americans. Recent polls indicate as many as two-thirds of voters disapprove of President Trump’s handling of the eight-month conflict, which has driven up prices and depleted U.S. ammunition stockpiles.

Yet in the final days of the campaign, Mr. Trump kept talking about it.

“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters on Saturday.

“The only reason we’re not finished with Iran is, I want to be nice, I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” he said at a campaign rally on Sunday.

“We had a war with Iran,” he added Monday. “We won.” Hours later, officials confirmed that the U.S. military had struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what they described as a defensive measure that was not expected to escalate.

Here are three reasons why Mr. Trump kept bringing up Iran, according to analysts.

Mr. Trump, who prides himself on his deal-making, could be trying to restart talks.

“By threatening strikes, he wants to send the Iranians a message: ‘Come to the table now or else,’” said Arta Moeini, managing director of the nonpartisan Institute for Peace and Diplomacy, which advocates for military restraint.

Iran’s foreign ministry on Monday said it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the United States agreed to several demands, including lifting U.S. economic sanctions against Iran and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets.

The Trump administration is unlikely to accept either condition. For now, Mr. Trump “is going to use the promise of diplomacy again, as he has done before,” Mr. Moeini said. “He can announce that, and maybe get better results for the election, but still later say, ‘They didn’t do what they promised to do, and so we can attack.’”

Threatening rhetoric is part of Mr. Trump’s brand and has helped him build a loyal following.

“There is a very real strand of American public opinion, the Jacksonian tradition, that likes a leader who projects toughness and who is prepared to whack the bad guys,” said Andrew Payne, a research director at Chatham House, a policy institute in London.

But Mr. Payne called that approach to Iran a “misguided” political strategy. “You’ve seen the polling,” he said.

Yet polling will matter less for Mr. Trump going forward. Regardless of the outcome of Tuesday’s elections, he will be entering his final two years in office, a period when presidents often take policy risks to secure their legacies.

“He has staked his legacy in foreign policy, to some degree, on Iran,” Mr. Payne said. “It’s more important for him to try and get some favorable resolution to that in the long term than worrying about the short-term impact at the polls.”

The Trump administration is already moving three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces to the Persian Gulf region, to be ready to strike within days.

“I do believe that he will escalate no matter what,” Mr. Moeini said. “I don’t think that’s cheap talk.”

item.title: America’s Arab Allies Brace for War as Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms
item.description:
In the marble-floored atria of a five-star hotel in Manama, Bahrain’s capital, military officers in full regalia mingled with ambassadors and political analysts last weekend, swapping business cards and chatting over plates of tiramisù infused with Arabic coffee.

The smiles and the warm handshakes at the gathering — the Manama Dialogue, an annual security conference — belied the grim topic underpinning much of the conversation. The possibility that the United States might, within days, reignite its war with Iran, prompting a barrage of Iranian missiles and drones on the very city where they were meeting, hung over the event like a dark cloud.

As President Trump weighs a renewed attack on Iran sometime after the midterm elections on Tuesday, Gulf Arab officials fear that their countries — which host American military bases, Western companies and valuable oil and gas facilities — will be the hardest hit, as they were after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. They also fear that the fighting will be worse this time around.

The Iranian and American positions on a potential deal to stave off a crisis are still “far apart,” Anwar Gargash, a senior official from the United Arab Emirates, told the conference audience. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”

The U.S. military carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, according to U.S. officials. Still, Mr. Trump told Fox News on the same day that “there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”

American and Israeli military officials have drawn up an expanded list of targets to strike, including energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy. Iran has warned that it would retaliate fiercely, targeting critical infrastructure and underwater communications cables in the region.

The Gulf countries are already bruised, working to repair energy infrastructure and radar systems that were damaged in the last round of attacks and coping with major economic disruptions. And while their governments operate advanced air defense systems and have worked to harden their defenses, they are constrained in their ability to fend off attacks by a global shortage of missile interceptors.

Saudi Arabia is also preparing for the possibility of a war on several fronts, as the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen fire near-daily volleys of missiles and drones at the kingdom, targeting airports and oil facilities.

The energy-rich Gulf countries have long marketed themselves to tourists and investors as safe havens in a volatile Middle East. Now, some citizens and residents are stockpiling water and cash, or preparing “go bags” full of emergency essentials to grab if they need to flee their homes. Others have changed their travel plans to return home as soon as possible, worried that they could be stuck outside the region if missile and drone attacks force countries to close their airspace.

While a preliminary cease-fire was reached in June — followed by several months of limbo and intermittent bursts of fighting — people in the Gulf fear that it is now “just a matter of time” before their countries get dragged back into a full-blown war, said Khalid Al-Jaber, executive director of the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, a research institute in Qatar.

“The scary part this time is that the war is going to be worse than before,” he said. “It’s going to be bigger. It’s going to be much harder for everyone.”

The past few days have been marked by a flurry of diplomacy and calls for de-escalation among President Trump’s closest Arab allies, including Saudi Arabia, which sent its defense minister to Iran last week to make the case for peace. Qatar has been leading an effort to reach a deal between Iranian and U.S. officials before it is too late, and in recent days Iranian officials have signaled that those negotiations have made some progress.

While Mr. Trump has said he would not attack before the midterm elections, he has hinted that all bets are off after that.

As a result, the elections have become a grim marker of time for people across the Gulf Arab states, many of whom know little about the American electoral system or the candidates running for office.

Instead, they know that before the midterms are over, they can reasonably expect their lives to continue as normal. They can drive to work and go to the mall, peruse Netflix on their phones and tend to their gardens with plentiful desalinated water.

After then, nobody knows what will happen.

“We are extremely worried,” Badr Abdelatty, Egypt’s foreign minister, said at the conference in Manama. “We have to push very hard in order to prevent the escalation. We are very confident that the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.”

Donald Blome, the U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs, told the audience at the conference that diplomatic channels between the United States and Iran were still active, even as the United States was “prepared to go in another direction.”

The event ended on Sunday, after which many of the attendees departed the region as quickly as possible.

Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

item.title: King Charles Says U.K.’s Role in Slave Trade ‘Fills My Heart With Horror’
item.description:
King Charles III on Tuesday expressed “profound personal sorrow” and “horror” over Britain’s role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, telling leaders of the country’s former colonies that the consequences of that history still “resonate with contemporary force.”

As expected, the king did not offer a formal apology for Britain’s trafficking of millions of enslaved people from Africa in the 1700s and 1800s. As the ceremonial head of state, he is constitutionally unable to apologize on behalf of Britain unless directed to by the government.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that he was open to a formal apology, in a major change of British policy.

King Charles added to his previous expressions of regret by acknowledging that slavery still casts a shadow over the nations that were once part of the British Empire.

“As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow,” Charles said in a speech in St. John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, at a meeting of the Commonwealth, a voluntary organization that includes 56 nations.

The king previously said that slavery “forever stains” British history, and he asserted last week that the country should directly “acknowledge the great suffering of the past.” His remarks followed years of pressure from leaders of the Commonwealth for Britain to apologize and pay reparations.

The king’s expression of royal contrition and Mr. Burnham’s shift in the government’s longstanding position on an apology for slavery are part of a concerted effort by both leaders to keep the Commonwealth from fracturing amid growing demands that Britain face up to its history.

Formed in 1949, the group of mostly former colonies is a remnant of the once-sprawling empire and a reminder to some of how much British influence has waned in the past century. As an organization, the Commonwealth has no real power, little money to distribute and a vague mission.

“It is time to admit that the Commonwealth does not only not serve its purpose, but works against its premise of post-imperial comity,” Ben Judah, who served as a top adviser to a former British foreign secretary, wrote on social media recently. He called for a restructuring of the organization.

But for many of the small, impoverished nations in the group, it serves as a forum to connect with their larger counterparts, including Britain, India, Australia and New Zealand. For Britain, the Commonwealth provides an opportunity to counter China’s influence on trade, investment, security and the environment.

“It allows us to draw on the collective ingenuity of a third of humanity to address the challenges confronting us all,” the king said in his remarks on Tuesday. “This, it seems to me, is the vital essence of the Commonwealth.”

In recent years, those opportunities have been overshadowed by growing demands for action — not just words — to address Britain’s slaveholding history.

Those calls grew louder in the past week, as the king traveled to the Bahamas and Guyana before arriving in Antigua for the Commonwealth meeting. On Thursday, hours before Charles met with Mohamed Irfaan Ali, the president of Guyana, Mr. Ali said in an interview that an apology for slavery should be “the next step.”

Mr. Burnham, who attended the Commonwealth meeting in Antigua on Tuesday alongside King Charles, tried to preemptively address those increasingly vocal demands last week.

In an essay in The Guardian, he wrote that his government was open to a structured conversation with countries affected by the trans-Atlantic slave trade, which he called “a brutal and barbaric violation.” Mr. Burnham added: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”

He rejected, however, calls for reparations, saying that British people should not be “held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

In Antigua, officials said Mr. Burnham would tell other leaders of Commonwealth nations that Britain is “open to discussions about the past.”

British government officials said a formal apology could emerge after the dialogue with Commonwealth nations. The BBC reported that could be within the next year, perhaps when Britain holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 countries.

For Mr. Burnham, the issue is a politically tricky one back home, where he has focused the early part of his premiership on addressing the rising cost of living and the need to rebuild the country’s social safety net.

Polls suggest a majority of people are open to a discussion about an apology. But many Britons say they do not believe current government funds should be used to pay for the sins of a long-ago government at a time when their own economic fortunes are declining.

It is not clear whether Mr. Burnham’s gesture — to move toward an apology while rejecting reparations — will completely satisfy either the Commonwealth nations or his own constituents. Speaking to reporters, Mr. Burnham drew a distinction between his opposition to reparations and his support for helping the economies of struggling nations.

“I’ve been very clear that we do not support reparations,” he said. “But it’s not the case that we don’t support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they’ve got.”

On Tuesday, the prime minister is expected to announce an effort to help Commonwealth nations restructure their debt, allowing them to pay over a longer period and at lower interest rates. In his essay last week, he said that he had asked Gordon Brown, a former British prime minister and a long-serving chancellor of the Exchequer under Tony Blair’s premiership, to attend the meeting on Tuesday and lead the debt talks.

Mr. Burnham will also announce a task force to encourage the development of critical minerals, his office said. And he will promise that Britain will invest 40 million pounds (about $53 million) over the next three years to accelerate critical infrastructure investment in the Caribbean.

Leaders of Commonwealth nations are likely to welcome those announcements. But they fall short of the ongoing demands from some countries that Britain make monetary compensation to the descendants of enslaved people.

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said on Saturday that Mr. Burnham’s openness to an apology was welcomed. But she did not back away from demands for reparations.

“On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she wrote in a statement.

After addressing the slavery issue, King Charles focused most of his Tuesday speech on opportunities and challenges for the Commonwealth nations.

“What unites this extraordinary and unique group of countries even more deeply is our values,” the king said. “Of democracy and the rule of law; of respect, equal dignity and human rights; of sustainable development; of peace and security. These values have never been more important, contested as they are on so many fronts.”

The king did not shy away from acknowledging the turmoil across the world.

“All around us, trust between nations is under critical strain, as international norms and systems are tested to their limits,” he said. “Brutal conflict stalks our world, destroying lives and casting long shadows across the globe.”

But he also expressed optimism about the future, noting a nature initiative intended to help protect biodiversity and increase conservation. He talked about plans for an insurance mechanism to help countries become more climate-resilient and to deal with natural disasters. And he endorsed efforts to bring heads of governments, investors and business leaders together to increase development in small economies.

item.title: Bomb Threats Disrupt Several Flights Across Europe
item.description:
Bomb threats targeted at least 7 planes in Europe on Tuesday, briefly disrupting flights as the local authorities carried out security checks at several airports.

All of the planes landed safely, and officials said that no explosives had been found. It was not immediately clear who had made the threats, how they were issued or whether there was any connection between them. The threats came a day after a midair bomb scare forced a plane leaving London to make an emergency landing in Budapest.

Anxiety over airspace security is high in Europe, where a spate of hybrid warfare attacks and intimidation tactics have rattled air travel in recent months as Russia’s war against Ukraine spills over its borders. Last month, an airport in Germany briefly shut down after a false alarm about a possible hijacking on an incoming flight from Greece.

Here are where the threats were reported.

Polish officials responded to “an alarm regarding a bomb threat on board” a plane traveling from London just before 10 a.m. on Tuesday, Warsaw Modlin Airport said in a statement on social media.

The plane landed minutes later at Modlin, which mostly serves budget airlines and is northwest of the capital, instead of the larger Warsaw Chopin Airport, its intended destination, the statement said.

Officials and pyrotechnic teams met the plane, which was carrying 181 people, and Modlin temporarily ceased operations. After noon, the bomb alert was “canceled,” the airport said.

A flight traveling from Copenhagen to Warsaw and operated by the Scandinavian airline SAS was also targeted by a threat, according to the airline.

The aircraft landed normally and the passengers disembarked, Alexandra Lindgren Kaoukji, a spokeswoman for SAS, said in an email. She said the police in Warsaw were now handling the matter.

In response to a bomb threat, the police in the southern city of Murcia inspected a plane that had traveled from Manchester, England but “ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane,” said Francisco Lucas, a local Spanish official. There were 114 passengers and seven crew members on board.

Mr. Lucas said on social media that Murcia’s international airport had resumed normal operations after the threat.

The Bulgarian transportation ministry said that two planes targeted by bomb threats landed in Sofia, the capital, on Tuesday, but that officials found no explosive devices on board.

One plane was a Wizz Air flight coming from Italy, while the other was a Ryanair flight from Dublin, the ministry said in a statement.

Two Ryanair flights arriving at Fiumicino Airport in Rome were disrupted by bomb scares, the airport press office said in an email. One came from Lisbon and the other flew in from Dublin.

The Roman airport authorities said that there had been “an anonymous report of a suspected bomb on board” the flight coming from Lisbon. Police bomb disposal experts assessed the situation, and the alert was lifted.

The flight from Dublin was escorted to the airport by the Italian Air Force, the airport said. After security checks, no explosives were found.

There were about 300 people on board the two flights, including passengers and crew, the airport said. “The relevant authorities are investigating the origin of the threats,” it said.

item.title: Poland Beefs Up Security at Border With Russia
item.description:
Poland has launched a “special operation” involving counterterrorism police, intelligence officers and beefed-up border security on its northern frontier with Russia, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, calling it a response to “disturbing movement” that could be preparation for “armed incursions.”

Mr. Tusk, speaking in Warsaw, said the late-night movement just across the border in Kaliningrad — a Russian region sandwiched between Poland, the Baltic Sea and Lithuania — involved unidentified people carrying flashlights, whose intentions were not clear.

He said Poland had received warnings from allied intelligence services of possible “acts of sabotage or more serious provocations on the border with the Russian Federation.” Mr. Tusk added that “more precise information,” received recently, indicated that “events could occur in the first half of November, including armed incursions” into Polish territory.

“It’s not a coincidence that this tension, provoked by the Russians, is occurring today,” Mr. Tusk said, citing “global uncertainty and confusion” over the midterm elections in the United States and a “sense of conflict and instability” in Poland because of a bitter political dispute over its constitutional court.

European governments have been frazzled in recent months by a spate of sabotage operations that officials have blamed on Russia, including a failed drone attack on a German airport. There have also been warnings, citing intelligence reports, that Russia could be planning some kind of military incursion or provocation along NATO’s eastern flank.

An airport outside of Warsaw shut down briefly on Tuesday after a bomb threat was directed at a flight from London, one of two Warsaw-bound flights that were targeted in what appeared to be hoax threats. Several other flights in Europe were also subjected to bomb threats. All landed safely, and the threats were being investigated.

Some of Mr. Tusk’s political opponents accused him of using border tensions to distract attention from an effort by government-backed judges on the Constitutional Tribunal to unseat its chief justice, a supporter of Poland’s former right-wing governing party, Law and Justice. Mr. Tusk’s government sent riot police to seal off the court on Friday.

President Karol Nawrocki, a foe of Mr. Tusk and a vocal supporter of the chief justice, barely mentioned Russia at a National Security Council meeting held on Tuesday to discuss defense issues, focusing instead on the standoff at the Constitutional Tribunal.

While stating that “the aggressor,” a reference to Russia, “must be effectively deterred” even as it “operates below the threshold of war,” Mr. Nawrocki vowed to resist changes at the court and “stop this attempt to overturn the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland.”

Kaliningrad, formerly German land that was annexed by the Soviet Union after World War II, is Russia’s westernmost territory. As the headquarters of its Baltic Fleet and a major military garrison, it has long been viewed as a potential launchpad for military action.

Poland’s previous right-wing government, facing a tough election in 2023, warned that Russian mercenary fighters were mobilizing to seal off the so-called Suwalki Gap, which stretches from Kaliningrad to Belarus between Poland and Lithuania.

Once, closing the gap would have separated the three Baltic states, all members of NATO, from the rest of the military alliance. But Finland’s entry into NATO after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed that. The mercenaries that the government warned about in 2023 never appeared.

Far more likely than an armed incursion from Kaliningrad into Poland, according to analysts, are small-scale provocations and sabotage operations aimed at destabilizing Mr. Tusk’s government, which Moscow reviles because of its strong support for Ukraine and the European Union.

Disorder on the frontier, according to this theory, could help turn Polish opinion against Ukraine and boost right-wing political forces that are hostile to the European Union, Ukrainian refugees and, in some cases, military support for Kyiv. Most of the weapons and ammunition that Ukraine receives from the West pass through Polish territory.

Instability on the border could also stoke further political tumult amid rising passions over the standoff at the Constitutional Tribunal. Mr. Tusk’s opponents accused him of staging a “coup d’état” after the deployment of riot police outside the court, where five new judges appointed by Parliament had supported a move to unseat the chief justice.

The right-wing opposition insists that those judges are impostors because Mr. Nawrocki, the president, refused to preside over their swearing-in ceremonies. The president has no veto power over judicial appointments, but does have ceremonial duties, something that Mr. Nawrocki has used to try to block the new judges.

On Tuesday, Mr. Tusk tied right-wing denunciations of his actions to a campaign of similar attacks by officials and state media outlets in Moscow, apparently hoping that the deep suspicion of Russia shared by nearly all Poles would help rally public opinion behind his efforts to break the judicial deadlock.

Urging his critics not to become “useful idiots,” Mr. Tusk said: “It’s invaluable today that Polish politicians don’t intentionally or foolishly serve the interests of Russia, which relies on destabilization, disregard for international law, deeming the European Union its main enemy, and so on.”

Anatol Magdziarz contributed reporting from Warsaw.

item.title: West Bank Property Sales Tactics Face a Challenge in Canada
item.description:
Should consumers be told if so-called dream homes promoted for sale in a foreign country stand on land their government deems illegally occupied?

Six Canadians think so, and recently filed a complaint with their country’s Competition Bureau about Israeli real-estate roadshows targeting customers abroad. Some firms, the complainants say, deceptively tout properties in the occupied West Bank as if these were within Israel, obscuring legal, financial and other risks associated with the sales.

The complaint, a novel legal approach to the issue, follows protests over Israeli real-estate marketing tours in Canada, Britain and the United States in recent years. It comes as the Canadian government wrestles with how to respond to years of rapidly expanding Israeli settlement in the West Bank and the Israeli government’s failure to curb a rise in extremist settler violence.

About three million Palestinians and, as of now, about 500,000 Jewish settlers live in the West Bank, a territory Israel occupied in 1967 after a war with neighboring Arab states. Over the years, Israel has allowed settlers to build and expand the country’s hold on the territory, which some religious Jews consider part of a divinely promised homeland.

Much of the international community considers Israel’s occupation and settlement of the territory to be illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.

In September, Canada joined Britain and France in announcing it will ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements to underscore the position that Israeli occupation of the West Bank is illegal and undermines prospects for peace and establishment of a Palestinian state.

The Canadian government in August “strongly” advised businesses against “economic and financial activities associated with Israeli settlements,” warning of “significant legal, financial and reputational risks” in view of the occupation’s illegality.

The recent Canadian complainants argue that the Canadian government’s statements and actions highlight the threat to consumers who may be exposed to deceptive marketing. Some sales pitches and materials, the complainants say, obfuscate important information, giving Canadians the impression that investing in homes in the occupied West Bank is indistinguishable from buying property within Israel’s internationally recognized borders.

“Given the possibility that future Canadian measures could extend to settlement real estate or related services,” their filing states, “the financial and legal consequences for Canadian consumers interested in purchasing Israeli real estate that may in reality be located in Israeli settlements could be grave and far-reaching.”

When the location of properties in the West Bank is obscured, and the implications of purchasing there are not made clear, “there’s so much at stake for the Canadian consumer,” said Emily Schaeffer Omer-Man, the executive director of Global Echo Litigation Center, one of the nonprofits behind the complaint.

It accuses real-estate firms marketing to foreigners of a “pattern of false and misleading representations,” echoing the condemnation that such roadshows have drawn on multiple continents but targeting the approach using competition law.

In England, about 100 lawmakers in June called for the cancellation of traveling Israeli real-estate events, calling them inconsistent with international law. In New York, dueling protests took place when such events were held in May, with some demonstrators objecting to and others defending the presentations. The various Israeli road shows have also generated demonstrations in New Jersey and California, as well as in Canada.

The six Canadians bringing the complaint, primarily from Palestinian and Jewish communities, want competition-law enforcers to scrutinize the websites and other marketing materials of several businesses in Israel and Canada that participated in events in Toronto and Montreal between 2024 and 2026, and to stop any ongoing obfuscation by these firms and others.

While five firms are specifically named, the filing argues that the tactics of these businesses — including mingling listings of properties within and outside of Israel proper or referring to homes in settlements as “in Israel” — are representative of a broader approach by some property promoters that puts Canadians in peril. The five named companies did not respond to requests for comment.

Any six adult residents of Canada can apply to the Competition Bureau for an inquiry into claims of anticompetitive activity, including accusations of misrepresentation to advance business interests. The bureau must launch a formal investigation if the request meets technical requirements, Rosalie Leblanc, a spokeswoman for the Competition Bureau, said in an email confirming receipt of the complaint. But she declined to provide details, citing confidentiality requirements.

Pierre Larouche, a competition law specialist and law professor at the University of Montreal who was not involved in the filing, said in an interview that the complaint takes a “clever” approach to a fraught issue, though it is not guaranteed to succeed. While the backdrop is obviously political, the claim that businesses may be misrepresenting critical information to consumers about property location is a relatively straightforward legal matter within the Competition Bureau’s remit, he said.

The recent challenge to West Bank real-estate promotions — filed on behalf of the parties by Global Echo Litigation Center and Canadian Lawyers for International Human Rights — is reminiscent of a lengthy legal battle brought by one man in Canada in 2017 over wines produced in settlements in occupied territories that were sold as products “of Israel.”

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency ultimately ruled in 2022 that “Product of Israel” labels affixed to wines produced in illegal West Bank settlements were “false” and violated consumer protection law.

item.title: Deportation of Dozens of Afghans Blocked by Federal Court, for Now
item.description:
A federal court on Tuesday temporarily blocked the Trump administration’s plan to put dozens of Afghan immigrants on a plane and send them back to Afghanistan, where many fear they will face persecution by the Taliban.

Judge Valerie Caproni of the Federal District Court for the Southern District of New York said that the United States could not send any Afghan nationals to Afghanistan this week, but she was sparse in her reasoning and did not address the dangers the deportees might face upon returning to Afghanistan.

The Trump administration has detained dozens of Afghan immigrants in recent days, the most expansive step so far to include Afghans in its wider immigration dragnet. To carry out the deportation, the United States plans to fly the Afghans to Pakistan, which would then send them across the border to Afghanistan.

The deportation flight was set leave Alexandria, La., early this month, according to officials and court filings. The judge’s order now prevents any of the Afghans from being sent back until Sunday, when the block expires. But it does not put an end to the deportations altogether.

U.S. law prohibits the government from deporting people to countries where courts have ruled they would most likely face persecution or torture. It isn’t known whether any of the Afghans set for deportation have any individual court protections.

After The Times published its story on the planned deportation, 66 Congressional Democrats signed a letter on Monday calling for the State Department and Department of Homeland Security to cancel the flight. “Sending dozens of people back to one of the most dangerous countries on earth, and where they are likely to be targeted for their or their family’s suspected support of U.S. government or criticism of the Taliban, is a death sentence,” the letter said.

The administration has argued in court cases that some of the people fighting deportation to Afghanistan have already exhausted their legal options and that the courts’ authority to intervene now is limited.

Among the more than 150 Afghans targeted for mass expulsion is at least one woman, according to court filings obtained by The New York Times and a U.S. official, as well as at least one gay man and relatives of those who helped the U.S. military, The Times reported last week. Homosexuality is punishable by death in Afghanistan, and women have faced severe restrictions on work, travel and education. Beyond that, when the Taliban returned to power in 2021, those who helped U.S. forces were sometimes singled out for retribution.

Federal judges have put some significant roadblocks in the way of the administration’s plan, with decisions on individual deportations. On Monday, a judge delayed the deportation of a man whose wife worked with the U.S. military, by 14 days, his lawyer said. On Tuesday, a judge ordered the immediate release of the gay man. Both said they feared for their lives if they are returned to Afghanistan.

The Afghan woman, who was detained at the southern border in 2025 after entering the United States illegally, is Christian and worked as a journalist for a radio station in Afghanistan, according to court filings and her attorney.

The woman’s lawyers argued in an emergency court filing on Monday that her religious identity and work as a journalist would make her a target for persecution by the Taliban. Two of her colleagues at the station were killed in 2019 by unidentified gunmen.

The Taliban has imposed some of the harshest restrictions on women in the world, and hers would be one of the few known cases of a woman deported by the United States to Afghanistan. In September, an Afghan woman accused of supporting the Islamic State was sent back in the first successful use of an obscure court set up three decades ago to deport immigrants with ties to terrorist groups. She eventually agreed to the removal.

A spokesman for the Department of Homeland Security said that ICE “does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations or individual case details.”

Some of the lawyers trying to stop the deportations argue that by transferring the Afghans to Pakistan, the United States is deporting people to a third country, one now at war with Afghanistan. That conflict, in addition to Afghanistan’s repressive Taliban government, they claim, puts the migrants at risk of torture or persecution, in violation of international treaties to which the United States is a party. Judge Caproni, in her order Tuesday, did not weigh in on that question.

Pakistan has deported or forced to return more than 2.7 million Afghans since 2023. Many have faced harassment and intimidation before being forced back into Afghanistan.

The Pakistani military did not respond to a request for comment on Pakistan’s exact role in the U.S. deportation plan.

In one court filing, the Trump administration disputed that deportations to Afghanistan via Pakistan amounted to third-country deportations because the immigrants would ultimately return to their country of origin after “transiting through” Pakistan.

A 2025 memo from the Homeland Security Department states that before receiving third-country deportees from the U.S., foreign governments must give credible “diplomatic assurances” that they will not be persecuted or tortured. Some of the lawyers for the detainees who are challenging their removal via Pakistan argue that there is no evidence that such assurances have been provided in their cases.

Even if the detainees’ lawyers were able to establish that the unusual arrangement with Pakistan amounted to a third-country deportation, that might not be sufficient to persuade the courts to intervene. In September, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration’s third-country deportation effort to continue by blocking a ruling from a lower-court judge that required more due process. Some district court judges have interpreted it as giving a green light to third-country deportations, at least for now.

Taliban officials responded to the planned deportation with social media posts expressing concern about sending Afghan citizens to Pakistan and offering to arrange for the return of Afghan citizens directly.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration has restricted immigration for Afghans who helped the American war effort, deported others to countries in Africa, and pushed some, who are stranded in a former U.S. military camp in Qatar, to return to Afghanistan voluntarily.

“If this works through Pakistan, the playbook is set: Send people to a third country and let that country finish the job,” said Shawn VanDiver, the president of the rights group AfghanEvac. “Once it’s done, it gets easier every time after, including for the people at Camp As Sayliyah,” he added, referring to the military camp in Qatar where more than 1,000 Afghans with ties to U.S. service, many of them women and children, have been waiting for resettlement for years.

The woman on this month’s deportation flight had represented herself in an application for asylum after coming to the United States in 2025, according to government and court documents. The case was pretermitted, or dismissed without a trial, under a provision that allows judges to throw out cases in which an applicant fails to fully answer questions on a screening.

The deportation, her attorney said in the court filing today, would carry “grave risk of persecution, torture and death.” The woman requested anonymity out of fear for her safety if she is deported.

Salehi, an Afghan man who is also scheduled for the deportation, entered America illegally in 2024, according to government documents. According to his asylum application, Salehi aided a resistance front at war with the Taliban and was arrested and beaten by the Taliban.

Salehi was denied asylum by an immigration judge and is preparing to file a challenge to his deportation. He requested he be identified only by his last name out of fear for his safety.

“This is the end for me,” he said in an interview from prison. “I can’t even imagine what is going to happen if I return because of my last experience with the Taliban.”
